newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan women lose political clout.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan women lose political clout.

text.p: Nicaraguan women, who held unprecedented political power in the 1990s, have been relegated to the political sidelines in 1997 with the arrival of the new right-wing government, feminist leaders said on Friday.

When former President Violeta Chamorro left power on Jan. 10, Nicaragua was the only country in Latin America with a woman president; a woman vice president, Julia Mena; and a woman at the head of its top election body, the Supreme Electoral Council, Rosa Marina Zelaya.
In its National Assembly, 17 of the 92 seats were held by women and from 1991 to 1992, Miriam Arguello was president of the National Assembly.

Nicaragua's women hit a political buzzsaw in January when President Arnoldo Aleman's Liberal Alliance came to power. Men hold all the top power positions in the new government, with women being given the minor ministries of culture and social action, Angela Rosa Acevedo, vice president of the Nicaragua's Centre for Constitutional Rights, told Reuters.
Of the National Assembly's 93 seats now, 11 are held by women.

"There is a strong contrast between the two governments. Every time you see the representatives of the new government they are all men," Azucena Ferrey, a former congresswoman who now heads the Nicaraguan Women's Foundation, said.

Nicaragua's feminists, many of whom were forged in the 1979 revolution that toppled dictator Anastasio Somoza and the left-wing Sandinista government that followed, are struggling to figure out what happened.

Acevedo said that after a century of rule by authoritarion governments led by men, Nicaraguan women learned to participate in politics during the 1979 revolution, which opened the doors to them at the political and social levels.
In the 1990s, Nicaraguan women took the struggle to the next level and demanded a share of power, she said.

Chamorro, who governed from 1990 to 1997 at the head of the centre-right National Opposition Union coalition, reversed Nicaragua's tradition of strongman rule, providing a national reconciliation government, Acevedo said.

But women's participation in politics has had a setback in 1997, although "the Nicaraguan women's movement continues being one of the strongest in Latin America, but we have lost space in the political sphere," she said.
An indication of the government's attitude, Acevedo said, was that it planned to close the state-run Nicaraguan Women's Institute and replace it with the Nicaraguan Institute of the Family.
